title: How Trump made America less popular than China
gist: Yglesias reports Pew polling showing China is now viewed more favorably than the United States across Mexico, Canada and most major European countries, and attributes the reversal to Trump's Iran war, its global energy-price shock, and a "bad neighbor policy" toward allies. His key market-relevant claim: oil prices stayed below the expected $100+ because China single-handedly absorbed 74 percent of the global import reduction via rationing and stockpile draws, while the US net-exporter position and its bifurcated pipeline-versus-LNG gas market insulated most Americans from the shock.

insights.claim: Pew polling from summer 2026 shows China is now viewed more favorably than the United States in a wide range of countries including Mexico, Canada and most major European nations.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Soft-power inversion raises the cost of assembling allied coalitions for export controls and tariffs — a headwind for any US-led tech containment strategy.
insights.quote: In Pew polling from earlier this summer, China is now viewed more favorably than the United States in a wide range of countries, including Mexico and Canada and most major European countries.
insights.locator: But things have taken a pretty sharp turn lately

insights.claim: A core structural American advantage over China has been that China's neighbors — Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and even Vietnam despite a negative history with Washington — prefer alliance with a distant United States over Chinese regional dominance, a pattern with no counterpart among America's own neighbors.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The bandwagon-versus-balance choice is the asset being spent down; erosion shows up first in defense procurement and supply-chain alignment decisions in Asia.
insights.quote: Even countries, like Vietnam, whose historical relationship with the United States was quite negative seem to prefer aligning with a distant and relatively benevolent United States to being under the Chinese Communist Party’s thumb.
insights.locator: For a long time, most observers have seen this

insights.claim: Part of the favorability gap is polarization around Israel, with Israel itself expressing the most favorable views of the United States and several Muslim-majority countries showing the largest swing toward China.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Separates a conflict-specific component from the broader trend; the Israel-linked portion could partially reverse with a ceasefire, the rest is structural.
insights.quote: Some of this seems like polarization around Israel, with Israel itself expressing the most favorable views of the United States and a number of Muslim countries exhibiting the biggest gap in China’s favor.
insights.locator: Some of this seems like polarization around Israel

insights.claim: Trump's second term has featured threats to invade Canada that transformed Canadian politics, European governments wargaming a fight with the United States over Greenland, and recurring musings about invading Mexico to fight drug cartels.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Allied hedging behavior — European defense autonomy spending, Canadian trade diversification — is a durable second-order consequence that persists past this administration.
insights.quote: He’s got European governments wargaming a fight with the United States over Greenland.
insights.locator: And then there’s the bizarre “bad neighbor policy”

insights.claim: Damage to America's reputation with friendly countries goes underscrutinized domestically precisely because it is remote from voters' key concerns, even though it may be among the most costly long-term actions of the administration.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Because the cost is invisible in domestic polling, there is no political feedback loop to stop it — assume alliance erosion continues to compound unpriced.
insights.quote: None of this stuff is popular with American voters, but it’s also remote from their key concerns, so it gets less attention than purely domestic concerns.
insights.locator: None of this stuff is popular with American voters

insights.claim: Trump has inverted Teddy Roosevelt's "speak softly and carry a big stick" doctrine into maximum bluster paired with little substantive interest beyond personal corruption, producing manufactured conflicts such as the feud with Italy that began with a boast that Giorgia Meloni "begged" for a photo op.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Diplomatic ruptures with no underlying interest conflict are unpredictable and unhedgeable — country risk premia should widen even for ideologically aligned allies.
insights.quote: Trump has done something like the reverse, engaging in maximum bluster while in practice having little interest in anything other than personal corruption and his White House ballroom.
insights.locator: The anti-Roosevelt doctrine

insights.claim: Trump's provocations — calling Justin Trudeau "governor" of Canada, dispatching JD Vance to Greenland — are entertainment bits driven by his instincts as a reality-television host rather than by strategic calculation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: If provocations are entertainment-driven rather than interest-driven, they are poorly predicted by strategic models and better predicted by news-cycle attention needs.
insights.quote: one of the responsibilities of the job of being president is to act in a dignified and appropriate manner, not provoke international incidents for the lulz
insights.locator: I think this is why he gets really into these bits

insights.claim: After the Venezuela gambit succeeded, Trump generalized that every regime is as hollow and corrupt as Maduro's and assumed that killing a few top Iranian officials would force the survivors to cut a deal — an assumption that failed and left him floundering.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Decapitation-strike strategies calibrated on Venezuela underprice regime resilience elsewhere; expect longer-duration conflict risk premia in Middle East energy.
insights.quote: After the audacious gambit in Venezuela paid off, Trump seems to have convinced himself that every regime is as hollow and corrupt as Maduro’s.
insights.locator: The price of war

insights.claim: The Iran war's energy-cost shock has been politically damaging domestically because higher energy prices infuriate voters, making it a first-order electoral variable rather than a foreign-policy abstraction.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Gasoline prices are the transmission channel from Middle East conflict to US political risk; watch pump prices as the leading indicator of policy reversal pressure.
insights.quote: The ensuing war has been a big deal for Trump politically because it has pushed up the cost of energy in a way that infuriates voters.
insights.locator: The ensuing war has been a big deal

themes.theme: US energy insulation from the supply shock

insights.claim: Because the United States is a net exporter of oil and oil products, increased domestic production and energy income partially offset higher prices, so the supply shock's net damage to the American economy is much milder than for economies that import all or most of their oil.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: US equities and GDP are structurally less exposed to oil spikes than in prior cycles; the asymmetric pain sits in import-dependent EM economies and their currencies.
insights.quote: Notably, though, the United States is a net exporter of oil and oil products. So while the supply shock is still on balance bad for the American economy, it really is a balance.
insights.locator: Notably, though, the United States is a net exporter

insights.claim: US natural gas trades at effectively two prices — a lower pipeline price from domestic fields and a higher global seaborne LNG price — because liquefaction capacity physically caps exports, insulating most Americans from global gas disruption.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The Henry Hub-to-global spread persists only while liquefaction is the bottleneck; each new export terminal narrows US consumers' insulation and links domestic gas to global geopolitics.
insights.quote: there are basically two separate gas prices: the price of gas that can be obtained via pipeline from American fields and the higher global price of liquefied gas shipped by sea
insights.locator: With natural gas, we’re even more insulated

insights.claim: Limited pipeline capacity in the Northeast forces New England to rely on seaborne gas and pay the global price, making it the one US region fully exposed to the international gas market.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: New England utility bills and regional power prices are a levered play on global LNG; the region is the domestic proxy for European gas risk.
insights.quote: Limited pipeline capacity in the Northeast means that New England relies on seaborne gas and has to pay the global price.
insights.locator: Limited pipeline capacity in the Northeast

insights.claim: Trump's claim that "we don't need the Hormuz Strait" is only partly right: global oil prices still transmit into American prices and global gas prices affect part of the country, though Americans do pay less than consumers in Thailand or the Bahamas.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Energy independence limits but does not sever price transmission — hedges premised on full US decoupling from Brent are mispriced.
insights.quote: The global price of oil still influences American prices, and the global price of gas influences prices in part of the country.
insights.locator: Trump periodically tries to make this point

insights.claim: The relative insulation of the US from the shock makes American policy look worse abroad, not better, because countries like Chile and Bangladesh had their economies damaged by a war they had no say in while the US president brags about being less affected.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The asymmetric burden is itself a diplomatic liability, raising the odds of coordinated non-cooperation with US trade and tech policy from affected states.
insights.quote: That’s real rogue superpower behavior.
insights.locator: What Trump doesn’t quite seem to grasp

insights.claim: China single-handedly absorbed 74 percent of the total global reduction in oil imports through a combination of rationing and drawing down existing stockpiles.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The single most important number for oil: the price cap is being provided by finite Chinese stockpiles, so restocking or an end to rationing removes the buffer and repricing risk is to the upside.
insights.quote: China has dramatically cut oil imports, single-handedly absorbing 74 percent of the total global reduction in imports through a mix of rationing and drawing down its existing stockpiles.
insights.locator: The helpful Chinese

insights.claim: Global oil prices have spiked less than most observers including Yglesias expected — the consensus was that offsetting the lost output would require sustained world prices well over $100 per barrel.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: An explicit marker of a consensus forecast miss; the demand-destruction elasticity assumed by most models was wrong because a state actor substituted for price rationing.
insights.quote: It seemed like reducing global oil consumption by enough to make up for the lost output would require world prices well over $100 per barrel on a sustained basis.
insights.locator: One point in the hawks’ favor

insights.claim: China's export of affordable, high-quality electric vehicles is materially helping oil-importing countries' economic health and the environment, functioning as a second constructive contribution alongside its import cuts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Chinese EV penetration in oil-importing emerging markets is accelerating structurally during an oil shock — a durable demand headwind for crude and for Western automakers in those markets.
insights.quote: China has also been flooding the world with what seem to be affordable, high-quality electric cars, which is good for the environment and for the economic health of oil-importing countries.
insights.locator: China has also been flooding the world

insights.claim: Chinese motives for absorbing the import cut are opaque because the regime is autocratic and does not produce clear reporting, but the net effect is that China limited the global harm the United States caused.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Because the motive is unknown, the durability of the buffer is unknowable — treat the current oil price as conditional on an unmodellable policy choice.
insights.quote: The Chinese government is a repressive autocratic regime, and so we never get really clear reporting on exactly what their thinking is.
insights.locator: Well, China has dramatically cut oil imports

insights.claim: Yglesias defends the logic of both the Biden and Trump administrations' efforts to keep Chinese EVs out and prevent China from dominating the global automobile supply chain.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Bipartisan continuity on EV protection means tariff walls around Western auto markets are unlikely to fall regardless of election outcome.
insights.quote: I’ve defended the logic of the Biden and Trump administrations’ efforts to keep these cars out and prevent China from totally dominating the global automobile supply chain.
insights.locator: I’ve defended the logic of the Biden and Trump administrations

insights.claim: Blocking Chinese dominance of EVs or of artificial intelligence requires other countries to cooperate, and that cooperation will not materialize while the United States applies tariffs to everyone in an unprincipled way.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate tariffs undercut the very export-control coalition needed for AI containment — a policy contradiction that raises the odds Chinese AI and EV firms win third-country markets.
insights.quote: But to pull this off — or to achieve the comparable goal of preventing Chinese companies from dominating artificial intelligence — we need other countries to cooperate with us. And that won’t happen if the United States is slapping tariffs on everyone left and right in a totally unprincipled way.
insights.locator: But to pull this off

insights.claim: American frontier AI labs are the one genuinely formidable element of US primacy, and Trump's conduct has made that primacy look alarming rather than welcome, pushing a majority of countries to prefer the Chinese alternative.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Geopolitical backlash is an underrated risk to US AI labs' international market access and to allied willingness to adopt American models over Chinese open-weight alternatives.
insights.quote: he’s made American primacy look alarming to the point where few countries welcome it and a majority seem to prefer our rival
insights.locator: Trump mostly makes America look like a joke

insights.claim: Democrats will not campaign on the collapse in America's international standing this fall despite Yglesias judging it one of Trump's most egregious failures, because it lacks domestic electoral salience.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Foreign-policy damage will go uncontested in the campaign, meaning no political mechanism forces a correction — plan for continuity of the alliance-erosion trend.
insights.quote: This is, rightly, not what Democrats are going to be campaigning on this fall.
insights.locator: This is, rightly, not what Democrats
